title: Implement the merge sort algorithm, explain the divide and merge steps, and analyse its time and space complexity and stability.
keyPoints: Merge sort recursively splits the array into halves until each piece has one element, then merges sorted halves back together.
The merge step walks two sorted sub-arrays with two pointers, always taking the smaller front element.
It guarantees O(n log n) time in all cases: best, average, and worst, with no quadratic blow-up.
It is stable: equal elements keep their original order because the merge takes the left element first on ties.
It requires O(n) extra space for the merge buffer, which is its main drawback versus in-place quick sort.
Java's object sort (TimSort) is an adaptive merge sort that exploits existing sorted runs.
Merge sort is the basis of external sorting where data too large for memory is merged from disk.

s1_definition.oneliner: Split into halves until singletons, then merge sorted halves by always taking the smaller front element; always O(n log n) and stable.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Merge sort** – a divide-and-conquer, comparison-based sort with two phases: divide and merge.
- **Divide** – recursively split the array in half until each piece has one element (trivially sorted).
- **Merge** – combine two sorted halves into one sorted whole using two pointers and a temporary buffer.
- **Stable** – taking the left element first on ties preserves the original order of equal elements.
- **Guaranteed O(n log n)** – the splitting gives log n levels, each doing O(n) merge work, in all cases.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India splits a huge pile of transactions in half, hands each half to a colleague who splits again, and so on until everyone holds a single transaction. Then the merging begins: two people with sorted stacks lay them side by side and repeatedly pick the smaller top transaction to form one combined sorted stack. Because they never reorder equal transactions, the process is both fast and preserves chronological order.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Merge sort is a divide-and-conquer algorithm that splits the array into halves until each piece has one element, then merges sorted halves back together. The merge step walks two sorted sub-arrays with two pointers, always taking the smaller front element, and taking the left element first on ties to preserve stability.

Its great advantage is guaranteed O(n log n) time in all cases, with no quadratic worst case. The cost is O(n) extra space for the merge buffer. The merge's sequential access pattern also makes it the natural choice for external sorting, where data too large for memory is merged from disk.

In a banking system at the National Bank of India, merge sort ensures transaction records are sorted by amount while preserving the original arrival order among equal amounts, which downstream reconciliation depends on. The predictable O(n log n) time meets strict latency guarantees.

Java's TimSort for object arrays is an adaptive merge sort that exploits existing sorted runs, combining merge sort's guarantees with insertion sort's efficiency on small subarrays. For general-purpose stable sorting with no worst-case risk, merge sort is the right foundation.

Remember one sentence: merge sort splits, merges with two pointers, guarantees O(n log n) in all cases, and is stable because it takes the left element first on ties.
